name: Zoe Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't go with any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Brook Lane, a community farm owned by about four hundred members as a co-op. We've two hundred ewes, a few pigs and a market garden that fills the veg boxes we deliver on Thursdays. My mornings are sheep checks and the afternoons are weeding leeks or packing boxes in the old dairy. I love the packing shed chat, and I hate my knees after a day on the onion beds.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. Before that I was a school cook for fifteen years, until the council handed the kitchens to a catering firm and they cut us to term-time only. Bridget, the farm manager, took me on even though I couldn't tell a ewe with foot rot from a lazy one. My partner Dev drives a parcel van, and we've got Asha, who's fourteen, and Ronnie, who's ten, and a mortgage on a terrace off Station Road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and I'd say it at the packing table with a grin. I use one of those chat apps now and then to tidy up the box newsletter, and it's handy but it's no miracle. Online I'd share something about putting the money into the NHS or schools instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly the same worries as now. Veg box orders dropped from two hundred and ten to one hundred and seventy last winter, and Bridget's said straight out that hours follow the boxes. My job's probably safe, but the money's tight every month whatever the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and put my name down for the lambing night shifts, because they pay a bit extra. I'd keep the newsletter going and try to win back some of the box customers we lost. And I'd move our electricity to the cheaper tariff that Dev keeps meaning to sort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit flat. It's the normal worry, the kind you carry in your coat pocket. I'm not scared, just tired of doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money pinch most right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: School shoes and the car, every time. Asha grew two sizes this year and Ronnie wrecks his. We've had one month of savings at most since I left the school kitchen, and that month never stays put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the co-op itself on solid ground?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Solid enough, I think, though I'm not in the finance meetings. The members are loyal, and a lot of them would rather pay more than see us shut. But loyal isn't the same as rich, and that's what I'd tell anyone who asked.

say: I'd say AI was **no miracle**, just handy for tidying the **box newsletter**.
I'd say the money should go into **schools and hospitals** instead.
think: I think my job is **probably safe**, but hours follow the **box orders**.
I think money stays **tight every month** whatever happens with robots.
do: Sign up for the **lambing night shifts** that pay a bit extra.
Win back lost **box customers** through the newsletter.
Switch the electricity to a **cheaper tariff** this winter.
feel: She feels **flat** and tired of doing sums, but **not scared**.
S0.quote: We've had one month of savings at most since I left the school kitchen, and that month never stays put.
fieldNote: She treats AI Plateau as **ordinary life**: the worries are school shoes, the car and falling box orders.
Her savings have **never passed a month** since she lost the school kitchen job.
She trusts the **co-op members' loyalty** but knows loyalty doesn't pay wages.

steps.text: Sign up for paid lambing night shifts in spring
Switch the household electricity to the cheaper tariff
Keep writing the box newsletter to win back customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one is coming for the office jobs and the van jobs first, not for people pulling leeks. I'd say the co-op should have a members' vote before anyone buys software that cuts a job. Online I'd share stuff about protecting workers, like I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm more worried about Dev than me. His parcel company already plans his route with a computer, and if it starts booking and answering customers too, they'll squeeze drivers harder. On the farm, the box ordering will go to an app, and that's the bit I do on Thursdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign Dev and me up for the union, him with the drivers and me with the farmworkers. I'd ask Bridget if I could learn the new box ordering app properly, since I already use the chat thing now and then. And I'd put twenty pounds a week aside, even if it's only twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a little knot about Dev. I can feel the ground shifting but I'm still standing on it. It's like the year the kitchens were outsourced, when you know something's coming and nobody's saying when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own work would you lose first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Thursday box orders and the customer emails, about a fifth of my week. Picking and packing stays with me, because no app is pulling up a beetroot. Losing the Thursday order desk to an app would cost me a day of hours, not my job, and I could live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev if his route got squeezed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't wait for them to call you in, start asking around now. Dev's the kind who keeps his head down and hopes. I'd be the one pushing, and we'd probably argue about it over tea.

say: I'd say this hits **office and van jobs** before people pulling leeks.
I'd push for a **members' vote** before the co-op buys job-cutting software.
think: I think **Dev's parcel job** is more at risk than mine.
I think the **Thursday box orders** I handle would move to an app.
do: Join the **union**, me with farmworkers and Dev with the drivers.
Ask Bridget to train me on the **box ordering app**.
Save **twenty pounds a week**, even if it's only that.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, with a knot of worry about **Dev**.
S1.quote: Losing the Thursday order desk to an app would cost me a day of hours, not my job, and I could live with that.
fieldNote: Her worry centres on **Dev's van job**, a household earner, more than her own.
She expects to lose about a **fifth** of her week to the ordering app, not her job.
She'd use the **co-op's member vote** as her lever, which most farmworkers don't have.

steps.text: Join the farmworkers' union and get Dev into the drivers' union
Learn the new box ordering app with Bridget
Put twenty pounds a week into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government has to step in, full stop. At the co-op I'd stand up at the members' meeting and ask what the plan is for the staff. Online I'd be angry, which isn't me, but I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 Dev's company can plan, book and answer everything without a person, and the vans might drive themselves not long after. By 2031 a robot can weed my leeks and shear my ewes. My partner Dev and I could both be out of work inside five years, and our mortgage has twenty-one years left on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd ask the co-op to write down that no job goes to a robot without a members' vote. I'd look at the adult course in sheep health at the college in Larkhill, since a robot still needs someone who knows when a ewe's poorly. I'd ask the bank about switching the mortgage to interest-only for a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. I keep thinking about Asha starting her exams the same year Dev's van goes driverless. I don't sleep well picturing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the co-op actually do, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the members would want to keep people, because that's half of why they joined. But if a robot weeder costs less than me and the box price has to stay low, I don't know how long that lasts. Bridget would fight for us, and Bridget doesn't have the final say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Asha and Ronnie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Mum and Dad are sorting it and they're not to worry. Then I'd tell Asha to do the subject she loves, because I don't think anyone knows which jobs are safe. I'd lie a bit about the money, if I'm honest.

say: I'd say this is **too fast** and the government has to **step in**.
I'd ask the members' meeting what the **plan for staff** is.
think: I think Dev and I could **both lose work** within five years.
I think the **twenty-one years** left on our mortgage would be impossible.
do: Ask the co-op to promise **no job cuts** without a members' vote.
Enrol in the **sheep health course** at Larkhill college.
Ask the bank about **interest-only** on the mortgage for two years.
feel: She feels **properly scared** and doesn't sleep well picturing it.
S2.quote: My partner Dev and I could both be out of work inside five years, and our mortgage has twenty-one years left on it.
fieldNote: Both household jobs are hands-on, so the **three-year gap** to robots is the only buffer they get.
She sees the **co-op structure** as protection but admits cheap robots could overrule loyalty.
She'd **shield the children** from the money truth, and says so openly.

steps.text: Ask the co-op to require a members' vote before any job goes
Enrol in the sheep health course at Larkhill college
Ask the bank about two years of interest-only payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's plan it like grown-ups. I'd put a motion to the co-op that the farm trains staff to run whatever machines come. To friends I'd say get your skills sorted before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I can finish the sheep health course and maybe the robot side of things too. Dev's van is the bigger worry, because the thinking bit of his job goes in 2031 and the driving soon after. Five years is long enough for me to retrain, but Dev (her partner) would need every one of those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the sheep course next September and do it one evening a week. I'd push Dev to look at the bus company, since they'll want people on board longer than parcels will. We'd put any lambing shift money straight on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less frozen than with two years. I can make a plan with five years. I'd still feel it every time I see a delivery van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools more, with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, once I see Bridget and the others using it for something real, like the flock records. I'm not first in the queue, but I'm not last either. If it helps me keep my job, I'll learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kenny, the pig man, who's sixty and won't even use a phone. Kenny's brilliant with the sows. I'd worry Kenny gets left behind and the members feel sorry but do nothing.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to plan this like grown-ups.
I'd put a **co-op motion** to train staff on the new machines.
think: I think five years is **enough for me** to retrain.
I think **Dev's van job** would need every one of those years.
do: Start the **sheep course** next September, one evening a week.
Push Dev to look at the **bus company**.
Put **lambing shift money** straight on the mortgage.
feel: She feels **anxious but less frozen** than with two years.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough for me to retrain, but Dev (her partner) would need every one of those years.
fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a **training plan**, but Dev's job remains the weak point.
She'd adopt AI tools **once colleagues prove** them on real work like flock records.
She worries about **Kenny the pig man**, sixty and phone-shy, being left behind.

steps.text: Start the sheep health course next September, one evening a week
Put a co-op motion to train staff on new machines
Pay lambing shift money straight onto the mortgage
Help Dev apply to drive for the bus company

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and nobody should be caught out this time. I'd tell the co-op members we can be the farm that shows how to do it decently. Online I'd push for public money for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots by 2039 means I'm fifty-six, with Asha and Ronnie grown up and the mortgage nearly half paid. Ten years is the difference between a crisis and a career change for a family like mine. I'd still worry, because the savings are thin and Dev's job goes earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the sheep course and then the farm machinery maintenance one after it. I'd use the chat apps more for the farm records, once Bridget sets them up. I'd vote for whichever party funds adult courses properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Not happy, but I can see a road. It feels like the start of lambing, hard and long, but you know where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the co-op to do over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it to train every one of us on whatever comes, and give us first refusal on the new jobs. Maybe a share of whatever the robots save. That's what a co-op is for, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd stop doing, with ten years ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop telling myself the farm job is forever. I've got to treat it like the school kitchen, good while it lasts. I'd keep an eye on the jobs board every month, not just when I'm frightened.

say: I'd say ten years is **fair warning**, so nobody should be caught out.
I'd push for **public money** for adult retraining.
think: I think robots by 2039 mean I'm **fifty-six** with the kids grown.
I think Dev's job still **goes earlier** and our savings stay thin.
do: Take the **sheep course** and then the **machinery maintenance** course.
Use AI tools for **farm records** once Bridget sets them up.
Check the **jobs board** every month, not only when frightened.
feel: She feels **steadier**, like the start of lambing: hard, but she can see the end.
S4.quote: Ten years is the difference between a crisis and a career change for a family like mine.
fieldNote: Ten years lets the kids **grow up** before robots arrive, which is her real measure.
She wants the co-op to give staff **first refusal** on new jobs and a share of savings.
She'd stop treating the farm job as **forever**, a lesson from the school kitchen.

steps.text: Take the sheep course, then the machinery maintenance course
Use AI tools for the flock records once set up
Vote for the party that funds adult courses

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Dev and I both do hands-on work and both lose it within five years. The worst picture for me is two vans and two pairs of hands all made spare in the same year. What would help is the co-op promising us training and first pick of new jobs, and the government paying for adult courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids' futures, not really. I'd want someone to say what Asha should study. Nobody can, I know, but I'd like someone to try.

headlineQuote: The worst picture for me is two vans and two pairs of hands all made spare in the same year.
portrait: Zoe is a **former school cook** who joined a co-op farm three years ago and is still learning sheep.
She and her partner Dev, a **parcel van driver**, live on thin savings with a mortgage and two kids.
She uses AI apps **now and then** and would learn more once colleagues show it working.
She worries most about **Dev's job** and leans on the co-op's **member vote** as protection.
Her mood climbs from uneasy to **alarmed** in the fastest picture, easing with ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both household jobs are hands-on and could go within five years.
whatWouldHelp: Co-op **training** with first pick of new jobs, plus government-funded **adult courses**.
